questions.q: What does the lesson say is the problem with treating 'it passed evaluation and shipped' as the end of governance?
options: A model that was validated once doesn't stay validated automatically, because the real-world conditions it's making decisions about keep changing
Models never actually need to be evaluated before shipping
Shipped models are legally exempt from any further oversight
Evaluation results become permanently invalid the moment a model ships
questions.explain: The lesson's core argument is that monitoring is what turns a one-time validation into ongoing assurance, since the world a model operates in keeps shifting.

questions.q: What are the four categories of signal the lesson says a production model needs monitored?
options: Volume, latency/errors, output distribution, and business outcome
Marketing spend, headcount, office location, and brand color
Only the model's file size, checked once a year
Only latency, since that's the sole meaningful signal
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists these four categories, noting the last two are the ones specific to governing a model rather than standard app monitoring.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say output distribution and business outcome monitoring are often skipped?
options: Because most teams monitor standard application metrics like volume, latency, and errors well, but the model-specific signals require more deliberate effort
Because they are technically impossible to measure
Because regulations explicitly forbid monitoring business outcomes
Because they are redundant with error-rate monitoring
questions.explain: The lesson notes teams are good at standard app monitoring (volume, latency, errors) but the model-specific signals are the ones most often left out.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what has to be decided before a model ships, not improvised after an alert fires?
options: Who is on call for the model's alerts and what actions they're authorized to take, such as rollback or escalation
The exact wording of the model's marketing description
The model's final accuracy score, which can be decided at any time
Whether the company will ever build another model
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that an on-call owner and authorized response actions must be defined in advance, or an alert is just an unread log entry.

questions.q: How does the lesson say the escalation path for an alert connects back to Lesson 13's model registry?
options: The owner field recorded in the registry entry is exactly who the escalation path should point to
The registry has no connection to monitoring at all
Monitoring alerts automatically delete the registry entry
The registry only stores training data, not ownership information
questions.explain: The lesson ties the escalation path directly to the registered owner captured in the model's registry entry from Lesson 13.
